name: Oxybenzone

lead: Oxybenzone is an organic sunscreen filter that absorbs UVB and part of UVA light. It was long among the most common sunscreen ingredients, and people use it to limit photodamage and keep skin smoother and more even-toned.

It absorbs UV photons between about 270 and 350 nm and releases the energy as heat. It is absorbed through the skin, was detected in about 97% of US urine samples tested in 2003-2004, and is linked in lab studies to coral damage.

paras: It is applied in sunscreens and lip products as part of a daily or beach-day routine. Its use in US sunscreens has declined.

Reported issues include skin allergy, systemic absorption, endocrine activity in lab assays and coral toxicity findings. Hawaii, the US Virgin Islands, Palau, Aruba and others restrict it. The FDA lists it as lacking sufficient safety data, but it remains legal.

angle.text: Oxybenzone absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA, so less photodamage accumulates and skin keeps a more even tone. The appearance case rests on sunscreen-class evidence for UV protection.

lead: Oxybenzone (benzophenone-3, BP-3) is an organic UV filter that absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA, used in sunscreens, lip products, hair sprays, nail polish and as a stabiliser in plastics [1][2]. It was first synthesised in 1906 by Bernhard König and Stanisław Kostanecki and later developed as a sunscreen ingredient from the 1950s, according to Grokipedia [1][2].

It is one of the most debated sunscreen ingredients. Biomonitoring found it in about 97% of US urine samples tested in 2003-2004 [3], clinical trials show it is absorbed through the skin [4], and laboratory work links it to coral damage [5]. Several jurisdictions, including Hawaii, have banned sales of sunscreens containing it [2]. In the United States the FDA classes it as not yet shown to be generally recognised as safe and effective because of insufficient data, while it remains legal [2].
infobox: EU 6% (face, hand, lip) / 2.2% (body); Canada 6%; Japan 5%; Australia 10% [2]

paras: Oxybenzone is valued by formulators for broad UV absorption, absorbing between 270 and 350 nm with peaks near 288 and 350 nm [2]. Grokipedia reports it was found in roughly 70% of sunscreens by the 1990s, while Wikipedia reports the share of US sunscreens containing it fell from 60% in 2019 to 13% in 2023 [1][2]. It also appears in foundations, such as a labelled US cosmetic product combining it with octinoxate [6].

Wikipedia summarises studies estimating that 0.4% to 8.7% of a topical dose is absorbed after one application, with higher absorption possible with repeated use [2]. A US survey (NHANES 2003-2004) reported benzophenone-3 concentrations in residents, detected in about 97% of urine samples [3][2]. Pregnancy cohorts measured urinary phenols including benzophenone-3 in relation to birth outcomes and offspring size [7][8], and a Puerto Rico study examined urinary phenol levels in pregnant women [9]. A 2020 JAMA randomised trial found oxybenzone in plasma after sunscreen use [4].

Reviews describe endocrine-related activity in laboratory assays [10][11]. A mini-review summarised occurrence, toxicity and ecological risk [12]. Wikipedia reports that photoallergic reactions are uncommon, though it is described as a frequent sunscreen allergen, and that Sweden's research council concluded it is unsuitable for children under two [2]. In September 2025 the European Chemicals Agency identified it as an endocrine disruptor, according to Wikipedia [2].

A 2016 study reported toxic effects on coral larvae and cultured coral cells and measured contamination in Hawaii and the US Virgin Islands [5]. Wikipedia notes that critics say many studies lacked controls or realistic conditions [2]. Sales bans or restrictions exist in Hawaii (2021), the US Virgin Islands (2020), Aruba and Bonaire (2019), Palau (2020), and marine parks in Thailand, while Florida's 2020 law preempted a local ban in Key West [2].

Clinical work centres on absorption and tolerability. The phase 1 absorption study enrolled 72 participants [13][4], a 1,000-participant photopatch study examined photoallergy to sunscreen ingredients [14], and several small SPF-testing studies of sunscreen products listed oxybenzone-era formulations [15]. Biomonitoring and exposure-reduction trials, including a 1,074-participant report-back intervention, address endocrine-disrupting chemical exposure generally [16]. No trial tests oxybenzone alone for appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: First synthesised by König and Kostanecki [2].
